documents.file_name: ATA36 - A350 PCE Leakage Monitoring Specification - ref ADNS V36SP2402319.docx
documents.content:
Record of Revision
Introduction
1.1 Purpose
Several reported damages on Engine Thrust Reverser Thermal Blanket and Pylon Thermal Blanket due to PCE (pre-cooler exchanger) leaks.

The root cause is an accelerated thermal fatigue caused by additional thermal cycles due to IP-HP switchings in cruise phase not foreseen in the design phase and a PCE leakage velocity above Thermal Blanket qualification levels.

Leaks in the PCE could damage the thermal blankets.

The model objective is to detect leaky PCE by measuring the depressurization time.


1.2 Definitions


1.3 References

Scope

Name of the model: PCE Leakage Monitoring
model ID: 
SPM: ATA36_XWB_PCE_LEAKAGE_MONITORING_M0
ATA 4D: 3611
2.1 Applicability

Aircraft type: XWB
Engine type: ALL
APU type: ALL
Equipment FIN: 7150HA1, 7150HA2
ATA 6D: 361162
P/N: 67200000-02
MOD status: N/A
SB embodiment: N/A
Other: The next S/W modification (not yet confirmed) will introduce a similar monitoring.
2.2 User Characteristics

Model type:
Support
SPM
Requested by 1YVS, 1SYPA and SBLK
2.3 Limitations

PCE Pressure Decay monitoring is not possible to perform during a Cross-Engine Start.
Monitoring Window duration when the second engine starts is limited by the OPSOV and MPV opening (EBAS starts).

System Description
3.1 System Overview

The PCE is used to reduce the temperature of engine bleed, before feeding it to the Air Generation Unit.

If hot air leaks from PCE it can damage the other components inside the pylon.

No active sensor is available to detect air leak from PCE.

At the end of engine start sequence pressurized air from APU is encapsulated in closed volume between MPV, OPSOV and SAV as highlighted in purple in the system diagram below.

PM1 sensor can be used to measure the pressure of this volume .

Small leaks are normal because the volume is not hermetic and the pressure is reduced gradually. However, in case of leaky PCE the air pressure drops drastically.


3.2 Failure mode description
Cracks in the PCE lead to faster depressurization of the air inside the volume. The air leaking from the PCE may damage the thermal blankets.
There is no Failure Message related to a leak in the PCE. The only way to confirm a leaky PCE is to perform a Leak Test to the component and check the status of the Thermal Blankets.
Model Description
4.1 External Interface Requirements
4.1.1 Data Source


4.1.2 Input Parameters
 

4.2 Functional Requirements
4.2.1 Internal or Customizable Parameters


 
4.2.2 Data quality checks

Check 1: All parameters available, otherwise “No Data Computed”

4.2.3 Features and logic computation

Preconditions 
ALL the following conditions must be satisfied for defining the monitoring window:

PM1 between 15 and 30 psig:
15 <= PM1 <= 30
HP6 between 20 and 80 psi and a minute ago was below 20 psi or NULL:
20 < HP6 < 80
HP6(1 minute ago) < 20 *
Engine running is 1 and 30 seconds ago was 0:
ENG_RUNNING == 1
ENG_RUNNING(30 seconds ago) == 0 **
APU Bleed Valve open:
APU_BV_FULLY_CLOSED == 0

* If the flight data starts less than 1 minute ago, it is 

Features
depress_time_raw = monitoring window duration in seconds

PM1_first = Value of PM1 at first point of the monitoring window

PM1_last = Value of PM1 at last point of the monitoring window

OPSOV_POS_first = Value of OPSOVPOS at first point of the monitoring window

OPSOV_POS_changed = Boolean indicating if OPSOVPOS changed during the monitoring window

pressure_drop = PM1_first - PM1_last

depress_rate = pressure_drop / depress_time_raw

depress_time = 15 / depress_rate

Invalid conditions

Invalid conditions (if ANY of the following conditions is satisfied):
depress_rate <= 0
pressure_drop < 3
(OPSOV_POS_first == 0) & (OPSOV_POS_changed == 0)

If there is more than 1 valid depressurization event in the flight, keep only the first valid depressurization event of the flight.

If there is not any valid depressurization event in the flight, “Invalid conditions” message is triggered.

Alerting

low_leak_event = depress_time < low_leak_threshold

high_leak_event = depress_time < high_leak_threshold


n_events_low = number of low_leak_event in flight_window

n_events_high = number of high_leak_event in flight_window


low_leak_alert: ALL following conditions must be satisfied
n_events_low > cumulative_events_threshold
high_leak_alert == FALSE

high_leak_alert: n_events_high > cumulative_events_threshold


Reset logic: Reset after maintenance action

4.2.4 Human Machine Interface [SPM only]

Items to be displayed



Performance Requirements
Performance Indicators

Expected results:
Valid flights: >95%
Valid flights producing alerts:
Low Leak Alert: 0.7%
High Leak Alert: 1.1%
Spurious alerts: 0%
Missed events: 0%
List of elements for model validation


Results dataset for validation: alerts_pce_pressure_decay

Prototype link

Prototype Data Lineage: A350_PCE_Leakage_Monitoring_Prototype

Appendix

MOCA: PCE Leakage Monitoring - MOCA

--- Diapositive 20 ---
Performance KPIs description
‹#›
See also algorithm performance KPIs proposal presentation (starting slide 7): 

Main measures (to help airlines make decisions when operating alerts):
Detection rate: proportion of actual failures that can be detected by the algorithm (in percent).
Confidence rate: probability that the algorithm is right when predicting a failure (in percent).
Anticipation time: duration between 1st alert generated by the algorithm and actual failure (in days).
Check min, max, median and distribution.

Secondary measures (to compare ease of use of competing algorithms):
Lag time: duration between A/C repair and algorithm alerts discontinuation (in days).
A positive lag means that the algorithm was not able to detect part repair or replacement autonomously.
A negative lag means that there was some cut-off, i.e. a premature alert discontinuation before the actual failure.
Jitter proba: indicates the probability that there is an interruption in algorithm alerting between the first alert and return to normal.
Gap duration: duration of interruptions in algorithm alerting that have been compensated (thus merging two or more alert periods into a single big alert period).
Check max to make sure merging of distinct alerts was reasonable.

Note:
Hide this slide during review.
Keep it in review presentation as a reminder.

--- Diapositive 21 ---
How to use KPIs
Detection rate: the objective is to have it as high as possible while staying good on other KPIs (especially confidence rate)
Confidence rate: should be 100%
If not possible then the acceptable confidence rate level should be agreed with the Front End.
Note: in some cases confidence rate may be adversely affected by jitter. You might want to check curves to know if confidence rate is due to real spurious alerts or just to jitter. Increase jitter_tol in the latter case.
Anticipation time: expected anticipation level must be agreed with Front End (typically 1 week).
Lag: must be < 1. (Lag is computed between reference event and first flight without alert after the event)
A lag of 1 may result from the tolerance added when computing KPIs to compensate for cases where only the date is available for events (and not the exact time of the repair).
If a lag < 1 cannot be achieved (typically the model cannot detect unit replacement by itself), then you will need to use the SPM model reset feature on maintenance actions declared by airlines.
A positive lag may also result from the airline operating for some time with the failure still present (in case of MEL application for instance) and/or from the choice of reference event date.
Jitter probability: Ideally it should be kept as low as possible. However some jitter is acceptable.
Cut off probability: should be 0% or as small as possible.
If the health indicator is closely correlated to equipment status, then it should steadily display a degraded state when approaching a removal.
However, noise may be your enemy and may result in an alert that stops triggering some time before the airline fixes the issue.


‹#›

Note:
Hide this slide during review.
Keep it in review presentation as a reminder.

--- Diapositive 22 ---

YuCCon module directly within your python code during preliminary design phase,

Model Perfo Tools within Foundry (recommended when assessing alerts generated by an SPM model).
Refer to:

--- Diapositive 25 ---
A350 ATA 36 : PCE Leakage Monitoring
Expected benefits simplified computation method
Compute the expected number of occurrences for one airline

np = Nb of aircraft in airline fleet x Nb of years considered x failure occurrence rate for the entire fleet found during targeted event search

Note: Nb of years considered should be set equal to 1 (maximum 3 as this is the horizon on which airline assess return on investment)

Check if algorithm is a good candidate for deployment
If np < 1.5, do not deploy the model to the airline (there is a high chance it will never trigger)
If 1.5 <= np <= 3, model may be deployed to the airline provided it has no spurious (any spurious will result in a non negligible chance of loss for the airline)
If 3 <= np <= 9, model can be deployed to the airline. A certain level of spurious may be acceptable. To be determined using the simulator.
If np >= 9 you can estimate benefits directly from the following formula:

Business value = ("single failure avoidance savings" x "yearly failure detection rate per A/C" - "spurious troubleshooting cost" x "yearly spurious rate per A/C") x "assessment period" (in years)

Proposed algorithm performance measures
Main measures (to help airlines make decision when operating alerts):
Detection rate: proportion of actual failures that can be detected by the algorithm (in percent).
Confidence rate: probability that the algorithm is right when predicting a failure (in percent).
Anticipation time: duration between 1st alert generated by the algorithm and actual failure (in days).

Secondary measures (to compare ease of use of competing algorithms):
Lag time: duration between A/C repair and algorithm alerts discontinuation (in days).
Jitter: interruption in algorithm alerting between the first alert and return to normal (probability and gap duration).
Cut off: premature alert discontinuation before part is replaced or deactivated under MEL.

Additional measures (to serve as inputs for business value computation):
Savings event probability per aircraft per year.

--- Diapositive 3 ---
ATA36_XWB_PCE_LEAKAGE_MONITORING_M0
Model history
AIRBUS AMBER
* For a model update, link to the previous model deployment review to be provided

--- Diapositive 4 ---
PURPOSE:
Several reported damages on Engine Thrust Reverser Thermal Blanket and Pylon Thermal Blanket due to PCE (pre-cooler exchanger) leaks.
The root cause is an accelerated thermal fatigue caused by additional thermal cycles due to IP-HP switchings in cruise phase not foreseen in the design phase and a PCE leakage velocity above Thermal Blanket qualification levels.
Leaks in the PCE could damage the thermal blankets.
The model objective is to detect leaky PCE by measuring the depressurization time.

SYSTEM DESCRIPTION:
The PCE is used to reduce the temperature of engine bleed, before feeding it to the Air Generation Unit.
If hot air leaks from PCE it can damage the other components inside the pylon.
No active sensor is available to detect air leak from PCE.
At the end of engine start sequence pressurized air from APU is encapsulated in closed volume between MPV, OPSOV and SAV as highlighted in purple in the system diagram below.
PM1 sensor can be used to measure the pressure of this volume .
Small leaks are normal because the volume is not hermetic and the pressure is reduced gradually. However, in case of leaky PCE the air pressure drops drastically.
Model description
AIRBUS AMBER

--- Diapositive 5 ---
FAILURE MODE:
Cracks in the PCE lead to faster depressurization of the air inside the volume. The air leaking from the PCE may damage the thermal blankets.
There is no Failure Message related to a leak in the PCE. The only way to confirm a leaky PCE is to perform a Leak Test to the component and check the status of the Thermal Blankets.

DATA SOURCE:
SAR Channel 17

MODEL LOGIC:
The model monitors the time it takes to PM1 to reduce 15 psi of pressure with the following conditions:
PM1 between 30 psig and 15 psig
HP6 between 20 psi and 80 psi
Engine Started less than 30 seconds ago
APU Bleed Valve open
Over-Pressure Shut Off Valve (OPSOV) is closed or closes during the monitoring window.

If the pressure drop is less than 3 psig or the depressurization rate is less than 0 psig/second, the monitoring window is considered invalid.

If there are more than 3 events in the last 5 flights with a depressurization time below 3 seconds, the model triggers a MEDIUM LEAK alert.
If there are more than 3 events in the last 5 flights with a depressurization time below 1 seconds, the model triggers a HIGH LEAK alert.

A350 ATA 36 : PCE Leakage Monitoring 














System Description
Background:
Pre-Cooler is used to reduce the temperature of engine bleed, before feeding it to Air Generation Unit.
If hot air leaks from pre-cooler it can damage the other components inside pylon.
No active sensor is available to detect air leak from pre-cooler


System Information:
At the end of engine start sequence pressurized air from APU is encapsulated in closed volume as highlighted in the Fig1.
PM1 sensor can be used to measure the pressure.
But all the components are not perfect including PCE(pre-cooler) and valves, hence air leaks out form the gaps reducing pressure gradually.
In case of leaky pre-coolers, air pressure drops drastically which is captured and is detectable by algorithm.

Leaky Precooler - Evidence
Fig1

Validation of ASR algorithm:
As explained in the system description section, the work performed for ASR focuses on developing an algorithm which captures depressurization time after engine start.
In normal conditions, depressurization time is >6sec
For abnormal cases when PCE is expected to be leaky, considering OPSOV, MPV, Engine Starter Valve are good and air pipes are not leaking, the depressurization will be very fast (<1sec).
As visible in Fig1, the algorithm have predicted leaky precooler from the Q1 2023 for MSN 54 of Singapore Airline (with sudden drop in depressurization time)
Early this year the hardware had be inspected and we found actual leakage in pre-cooler also thermal blanket around PCE is damaged.
This is a very good validation for proving the algorithm is working as expected.
After detection of leaky precooler the hardware is replace with new PCE on 13th Jan 2024

--- Diapositive 8 ---
A350 ATA 36 : PCE Leakage Monitoring 

Existing monitoring approach and how its useful
With the proven usability of algorithm and after discussions with airline (SIA).
Singapore airline is interested to continuously monitor the fleet performance.
In-line with this ideas, ASR work have been extended to develop a data analysis pipeline to continuously monitor the PCE performance.
Following is the dashboard which shows probably leaky precooler information.
Approach
Run the pipeline daily
Analyze flights from past 30 days for which sensor data is available on Skywise
Highlight the aircrafts with probably leaky precoolers

Dashboard

A350 ATA 36 : PCE Leakage Monitoring 

Need for monitoring at SPM
Why is there a need for SPM monitoring?
Operating with leaky precooler can damage other components inside pylon, especially in case of engine fire.
Singapore Airline is interested to perform continuous monitoring of the entire fleet.
Discussions with Qatar airline is in progress
The usability and validation of algorithm have already been demonstrated with ASR.
No new sensor or hardware change is required for implementation of the proposed approach.
Algorithm is very good at this point, multiple validations have been performed to validate by manually checking the depressurization time from time-series sensor data 

SPM monitoring will improve the prediction accuracy by tuning the threshold and logic.
SPM monitoring can cover the complete fleet of aircrafts
SPM will enable notification to airline in case of leaky precooler detection.
